name: Pedro Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a white van by the week and pick up parcels at half seven from the sorting yard on the edge of town. The courier app gives me a route of about ninety drops and a timer for each one. I'm still slower than the guys who've done it years; I lose time on flats with no buzzer. Saturdays I do food on my scooter to top it up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the radio on, sea air down by the harbour, and finishing early when the route goes well. Bad is the van hire, which takes almost a third of what I earn before fuel. I live with my girlfriend Lina, she's a receptionist at a dental clinic, and between us we cover rent but there's barely anything left. If the van breaks down, I don't earn, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like what the courier firms pay per parcel. I'd post something about how the van hire racket eats drivers alive. AI was the shiny thing, the van bill is the real thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the same treadmill. The routine stuff AI does, like sorting and route timers, is already in the app, so I wouldn't notice. My worry is still that ninety drops a day isn't enough to get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the route and keep the Saturday food shifts. I'd look into the drivers' association a couple of guys at the yard mentioned, because pay per parcel is the fight. If I could, I'd save for my own small van so I'm not handing over a third every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat. A bit stuck, like I'm running hard and the floor is moving backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the van hire takes a third of your pay. Does anything in this world fix that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, nothing fixes it except owning the van, and that needs a deposit I don't have. I've looked at second-hand ones on the forecourt by the bypass and even the rough ones are more than I could save in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clutch going. Last spring that happened and I lost four days and Lina covered the rent. A bad month means borrowing from my girlfriend, and I hate it every time.

say: The real story is **pay per parcel** and the van hire, not AI.
Van hire companies **eat drivers alive**, and I'd post that openly.
think: My life stays the **same treadmill**, since the app's routine AI is already there.
**Ninety drops** a day still won't get me ahead.
do: Keep the **parcel route** and Saturday food shifts.
Look into the **drivers' association** mentioned at the sorting yard.
Save towards a **second-hand van** to stop paying weekly hire.
feel: **Stuck**, running hard while the floor moves backwards.
S0.quote: A bad month means borrowing from my girlfriend, and I hate it every time.
fieldNote: The **van hire** is his central money problem, independent of AI.
Already relies on **his girlfriend** to cover rent after breakdowns.
Leans towards **collective action** on pay per parcel, not tech fixes.

steps.text: Keep the ninety-drop route and Saturday food shifts
Go to a drivers' association meeting at the sorting yard
Put aside weekly money towards a second-hand van deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms will use this to squeeze, so we need to stick together and push for rules. I'd tell people at the yard this is the moment to join something, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bit is safe for a while, I think, because someone still has to carry the box up the stairs. But the app will get even pushier with its timers. The bigger worry is at home, not in the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the drivers' association properly and pay the fee. I'd keep doing the route and pick up extra Sunday food shifts. I'd help Lina look for a job that isn't on a front desk, maybe at the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more for her than for me, which is a strange feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lina works on the front desk at a dental clinic. Where does this hit her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bookings and answering the phone, that's most of what Lina does at the clinic. If an AI takes the bookings and the calls, the dental clinic needs one person on the desk instead of two. My girlfriend is the newer one, so my girlfriend would be the one to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked a chatbot to help me write a complaint when the app docked me for a late drop that wasn't my fault. It helped. I'm not against it, I just want to see it work before I trust it.

say: Firms will use AI to **squeeze workers**, so drivers need to stick together.
Now is the time to **join something**, not later.
think: My job is **safe for a while**, because someone still carries boxes upstairs.
The bigger risk is **Lina's desk job** at the dental clinic.
do: Join the **drivers' association** properly and pay the fee.
Pick up **Sunday food shifts** on top of the route.
Help Lina look for **hospital jobs** away from a front desk.
feel: **Worried**, more for his girlfriend than himself.
S1.quote: If an AI takes the bookings and the calls, the dental clinic needs one person on the desk instead of two.
fieldNote: Thinking AI hits his **household** through his girlfriend's booking job first.
Uses chatbots **occasionally** and practically, once proven useful.
Plans **more shifts** as a buffer if household income drops.

steps.text: Pay the fee to join the drivers' association
Add Sunday food shifts on the scooter
Help Lina apply for hospital porter or ward jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper safety net, now, because this is coming faster than anyone can retrain. I'd post for a basic income and for taxing the firms that use the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina's job goes in 2028, I'm pretty sure. I'd have three years before robot vans and those little box robots on the pavement take mine. Three years on less than one month's savings doesn't feel like much of a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive every hour the app gives me and stop paying for things like the streaming service and the gym. I'd look at an electrician apprenticeship, because wiring and fixing things might last longer. I'd stand with the drivers' association on any action.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the tide coming in and I'm halfway across the beach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots around 2031. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to earn as much as I can and get a trade started. Robot vans need someone to fix them and load them, maybe. I'd use AI to help me study for the apprenticeship test, I'd be fine with that if it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lina we'd be okay, which might be a lie. Then I'd tell her we should stop talking about getting a dog and a bigger place for a while.

say: A **safety net** is needed now, because this comes faster than anyone retrains.
Firms using robots should be **taxed** to fund a basic income.
think: Lina's job goes in **2028**, and robots take mine around **2031**.
Three years with **under a month** saved is no head start.
do: Drive **every hour** offered and cancel streaming and gym.
Apply for an **electrician apprenticeship** and study with AI help.
Back the drivers' association in **any action**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the tide coming in halfway across the beach.
S2.quote: Three years on less than one month's savings doesn't feel like much of a head start.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** clearly and wants to use it for a trade.
Expects to lose **both incomes** in the household within three years.
Puts **family plans** like a dog and bigger flat on hold.

steps.text: Cancel streaming and the gym membership
Join any strike or action by the drivers' association
Put off getting a dog and a bigger flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same: use the time to put rules in place. Five years is enough for a government that wants to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can actually finish a trade before the robots come, around 2034. I'd be 35 and qualified. It's tight but doable, if I can live on apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrician apprenticeship in the first year and drive Saturdays to make up the gap. Lina and I would sit down and do a budget. I'd keep paying into the drivers' association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but with a plan. That makes a real difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is five years enough to finish an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, about four years for most. Apprentice pay is low, lower than the van, but there's no van hire. Paying no van hire might actually leave me about even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the yard would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Sam (a driver at the yard) won't retrain, and Sam's the one who taught me the shortcuts round the harbour. Sam's in his fifties and only knows the route.

say: **Five years** is enough for a government that wants to act.
Use the time to put **rules** in place for workers.
think: I could **finish a trade** before robots arrive around 2034.
Living on **apprentice pay** is tight but doable.
do: Start an **electrician apprenticeship** in the first year.
Drive **Saturdays** to fill the pay gap.
Draw up a **household budget** with Lina.
feel: **Nervous**, but steadier with a plan in hand.
S3.quote: Old Sam (a driver at the yard) won't retrain, and Sam's the one who taught me the shortcuts round the harbour.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **workable plan**.
Spots that dropping the **van hire** offsets lower apprentice pay.
His concern for an **older colleague** shows his solidarity streak.

steps.text: Keep Saturday food deliveries on the scooter
Write a monthly household budget with Lina

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody has an excuse. I'd push for the training to be free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'd probably wait a year or two and see what the others at the yard do first. That's how I am. Then I'd go for the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive another year or so, and try to save a deposit for my own van in the meantime. Then I'd do the apprenticeship. I'd watch what the others do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy that I'll put it off too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing at 37 in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Qualified sparky, my own small van with my name on it, maybe putting in chargers for the robot vans. That would be a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I keep saying next year. Ten years is long enough to waste five of them thinking you've got plenty.

say: **Ten years** is fair warning, and nobody has an excuse.
Training for a new trade should be **free**.
think: With a decade, I'd **wait a year** or two and watch others at the yard first.
Only then would I commit to the **electrician trade**.
do: Drive another year and save a **van deposit**.
Start the **apprenticeship** after watching what colleagues do.
Keep watching how **others at the yard** move.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to waste five of them thinking you've got plenty.
fieldNote: His **steady** style shows: he waits for proof before moving.
Self-aware that **procrastination** is the real risk here.
Dreams of **wiring chargers** for robot vans as an electrician.

steps.text: Watch what other drivers at the yard do for a year
Save a deposit for his own van
Train as an electrician after the first couple of years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Lina and I would both be out within three years. What would help is free apprenticeships with a living wage while you train, so I'm not choosing between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the van hire firms. Everyone talks about robots, but a guy renting me a van takes more off me every week than any AI ever has. Fix that and I'd have savings.

headlineQuote: A guy renting me a van takes more off me every week than any AI ever has.
portrait: Pedro is **27**, drives a hired van on a parcel route and does Saturday food deliveries.
The weekly **van hire** eats a third of his pay, so savings never build.
His girlfriend Lina works a **dental clinic desk**, which he sees as more exposed than his job.
He backs the **drivers' association** and leans towards an electrician apprenticeship once others prove it works.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both household incomes could vanish within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Free apprenticeships** with a living wage during training.
